This relatively modest oxygen consumption, placed in context with other phyllostomid frugivores, suggests an energetic economy that aligns with the species' reliance on seasonally available floral resources and protein-rich insect prey. The thermal regime under which these measurements were taken corresponds closely to the body temperature maintained throughout diurnal roosting periods, underscoring the bat's stable endothermic physiology. Metabolic data were collected from post-absorptive individuals during their inactive phase to ensure that the recorded values reflected true resting expenditure rather than the elevated costs of digestion or locomotion. These trials provide a critical baseline for understanding how Phyllostomus discolor allocates its energetic budget across key life history functions.

Reproduction in Phyllostomus discolor is characterized by an annual monoestry pattern, with females producing a single pup per litter [N_R_i = single pup per litter] and typically raising only one litter each year [F_R_i = one litter each year], both set against the backdrop of a body temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]. The combination of a single offspring and a single annual breeding event yields a maximum daily reproductive rate that is quite low compared to similarly sized small mammals. Field observations across several neotropical sites confirm that parturition is synchronized with peaks in local fruit and insect abundance, a seasonal cue that likely optimizes the survival of the altricial young. This low annual fecundity places the species firmly within the slow end of the mammalian life history continuum.

Neonatal pups of the Pale spear-nosed bat are born at a wet weight of 7 grams [Wwb = 7 grams], a modest size that represents a relatively small proportion of the mother's adult mass. At birth, these altricial young are nearly hairless and completely dependent on maternal warmth and milk, requiring intensive brooding during the first weeks of life. These size values are within the typical range for the genus Phyllostomus and reflect the generalist foraging niche of the species.

Longevity records for Phyllostomus discolor indicate a maximum lifespan of 9 years [am = 9 years], a duration documented in wild individuals and corroborated by captive maintenance studies conducted at a body temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C]. The long gestation combined with a single annual offspring and a decades-long lifespan creates a demographic profile characterized by low reproductive turnover but high adult survival, a pattern that makes the species vulnerable to population declines when adult mortality is elevated by anthropogenic disturbances.

Following weaning, juveniles enter a lengthy sub-adult period before reaching sexual maturity, with puberty attained at 280 days after birth [tp = 280 days after birth] at a temperature of 35.5 °C [T = 35.5 °C].
